Held 6–3 on 17 Sep; 74% priced for a hike at the November meeting
Hiked to 1.25% on 18 Sep; Reuters poll has 1.50% by end-March

events.note: June beat at +0.3% m/m; July is expected to slow. A soft print supports the Bank of England holding on the 17th.
A clean read on the value-conscious consumer.
Unchanged and exactly as forecast. The headline was not the story — core was.
Eased from 2.5% on the year even as the monthly rate accelerated. Base effects, not disinflation.
As expected. Energy added 2.1% on the month, gasoline 3.9%, fuel oil 10%.
The miss of the week: 0.3% against 0.2% expected, a four-month high. Airline fares rose 2.7% and owners-equivalent rent 0.2%. Services ex-shelter ran at roughly 6.3% annualised.
The index recently fell from 55 to 51. A sentiment read taken during a $100 oil print is worth more than usual.
Beat, led by high-tech manufacturing up 16.7%. Supply is fine; demand is the problem.
Missed, with auto sales down 18.5%. Fixed-asset investment contracted for a sixth month. Weak domestic demand, again.
Day one produces no statement. It matters only because the committee is now in the room and nobody speaks until Wednesday.
Missed on expectations, but the current-situation index jumped 14 points to −47.1, its best since mid-2023.
The bigger miss: sentiment fell where a sharp rise was expected. Five days after an ECB hike.
A clear miss — the softest since spring — and the dollar did not blink. On a Fed week the regional surveys do not get a vote.
As expected. First reading above 3% since March; motor fuels up 23% on the year did the work. Services held at 3.4%.
Unchanged for a fourth month. This is what lets the Bank of England hold tomorrow.
The one hot number in the UK set. Pipeline pressure from energy, and the reason two hikes are priced by year-end.
Import prices up 0.7% on the month and 7.0% on the year, the most since August 2022; non-fuel imports up 0.8%. The tariff channel is in the data.
Well above the 0.8% expected, and the biggest rise in five months; gasoline stations were 3.1% of it, but the control group rose 1.4% against 0.4%. The number that let the Fed hike without apology.
Ex fuel, autos, building materials and food services. The only retail line that says anything about the consumer rather than the pump.
Unanimous. Dots at 4.1% for end-2026 and end-2027, up from 3.8% and 3.6%; 16 of 18 see at least one more hike this year. Dow −1.21%, S&P −0.45%.
Warsh: hard-pressed to call conditions restrictive; the summer data did not tell him inflation had improved. Twenty-two minutes of questions and no forward guidance.
Headline a touch under consensus; core 2.4% as expected. The ECB hiked to 2.50% the week before regardless.

Held 6–3, three votes for 4%. Inflation 3.1% and rising, risks tilted further up than in July; gilt holdings to be run down to zero by 2034. Sterling fell to 1.3336 anyway; markets price 74% for a November hike.
An eight-week low, though the week held Labor Day. Continuing claims 1.73 million, the lowest since January 2024.
Fell less than expected from a very high August. Still comfortably in expansion.
Starts missed and permits fell 2.7% to 1.394 million. Mortgage rates near 7% are doing what the Fed intends.
A small rise where a decline was widely expected. Housing is soft, not collapsing.

Hiked 7–2 to a 31-year high, three months after the last move. Ueda: the phase has changed and the Bank will keep raising. The yen fell 1.18% on the day regardless; two dissenters were the prime minister's appointees.
A beat the morning after the BoE held. Ex-fuel +0.6%. Does nothing to argue against a November hike.
Vice Chair for Supervision. Two days after a unanimous hike, any hint on December is the headline.
The ECB hiked to 2.50% last week. Watch for anything on October.
The only US print of the day, so it will be traded harder than it deserves. Bowman speaks in London in the European morning.
A quiet close to a loud week.
No change expected. China's PMIs on the 30th matter more.

events.event: S&P Global UK consumer sentiment index (Sep)
Trump meets Gulf leaders at the UN General Assembly
events.note: The post-war plan for Iran, with the GCC, on the sidelines of the General Assembly. No published time — treat the whole New York session as exposed. Oil trades this headline before and after; a ceasefire is upside for equities and downside for energy, and the reverse.

events.event: Fed's Williams, Jefferson (14:20) and Barkin (17:00) speak
events.note: Three voters in one afternoon, the first full week after the hike. This is where the December hike gets priced or not.
Homebuilders have lagged the equal-weight S&P by 16 points since June. Guidance on cancellations at 7% mortgage rates.
Opens the global flash PMI run. Australia prints first because of the clock, not because it matters most.
France at 07:15 UTC, Germany at 07:30, the Eurozone composite at 08:00. Three prints inside forty-five minutes.
The first hard read on how the continent took two ECB hikes.
Half an hour after the Eurozone composite, and the first activity read since the Bank of England decision. Sterling trades the gap between the two.
August services printed 56.5, the fastest expansion since December 2020, manufacturing 53.9, composite 56.0. A strong flash is a hawkish print now.
The first activity read after the BoJ decision six days earlier.
The RBA meets on the 29th. A second monthly fall in employment would take a hike off the table.
Last week's 196,000 held Labor Day. A rebound toward 210,000 is noise; a second sub-200,000 print is not.
No clean consensus yet. July's 1.1% was the number to beat; core capital goods orders rose 0.2%.
The one-year inflation expectation, 4.6% in the preliminary, is the line the Fed reads.
Press conference at 05:30. Thursday's jobs print sets the tone.
The Fed cites this one directly when it talks about labour demand cooling rather than employment falling.
Trimmed mean 3.6% previous. The day after the RBA decides.

events.note: Both sub-50 in August. The RatingDog private PMIs follow at 01:45, previous 51.5 manufacturing.
The release the Fed named. Core PCE was 0.2% on the month and 3.3% on the year in July; the September dots assume 3.4% for 2026. A 0.3% month makes December a second hike.
Same print time as PCE, so it will be read through PCE.

howToRead.title: Impact is about how much price moves, not how much the number matters
howToRead.text: A high-impact release is one where the spread widens, liquidity thins and the first move often reverses. That is a statement about market structure at 08:30, not about economics. Plenty of important data is marked medium because the market has already priced it.

howToRead.title: The forecast is the level that matters, not the previous
howToRead.text: Price reacts to the gap between actual and forecast, not to whether a number went up or down. A 5.3% PPI print against a 5.3% forecast is a non-event; the same print against a 4.7% forecast is not.

howToRead.title: Two releases at the same minute are one event
howToRead.text: Agencies batch their releases, so you will often see three or four rows sharing a print time — jobless claims alongside the Philadelphia Fed, import prices alongside retail sales. Nobody trades the smaller one on a morning like that. When you see the same time twice, read the highest-impact row and ignore the others.

howToRead.title: A release-driven wick is not displacement
howToRead.text: Models built on liquidity runs misfire badly on data prints, because the move has no intent behind it — it is an auction gap. If your playbook has no rule about scheduled releases, this page is the argument for adding one.
